Investigation Lab — webshell-iis-001
  1 / 1
Start●

An alert fired overnight. Decide whether it is real.

no experience needed

Two security rules fired on your Windows servers on 22 September 2026, inside a quarter of an hour. This is the whole of what the first one said:

Alert 1, word for wordThe IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) spawned command shells (cmd.exe) that ran reconnaissance commands, and shortly afterwards the server made outbound HTTPS connections to an unfamiliar external IP.

That is one alert, and it is really two alerts glued together: the first half is a web server running operating-system commands, the second half is that server calling out to somewhere. Your instructor’s Security team raised them as two rules, and you will find five alerts in total when the lab opens.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last, and writing down what you find as you go.

The one thing you need first

Docker, installed and running — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The pieces

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. It might be nothing at all.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-2026.09.22 and network-2026.09.22.
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. It is a saved bookmark. Older versions called it an index pattern.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 273 in the auth pile and 147 in the network pile. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like process.name. The part before the dot is the group.
TimestampThe @timestamp field — when it happened. Everything in this lab happened on 22 September 2026.
QueryA typed question, like “show me events where the code is 4688”.
KQLThe query language the search bar speaks. and, or and not are written in lower case.
IISMicrosoft’s web server. Its worker process is w3wp.exe. It serves web pages; it should almost never launch a command shell.
Web shellA script an attacker uploads to a web server so they can run operating-system commands through the web. The tell-tale sign is the web-server process spawning cmd.exe.
Parent / child processWhen one program launches another, the launcher is the parent and the launched one is the child. This is the single most important idea in the lab.
ReconnaissanceCommands an attacker runs to learn about the machine they are on — who am I, what users exist, what is this box.
C2 / controllerAn attacker-controlled server that a compromised machine calls back to. Outbound HTTPS to one unfamiliar external address, right after web-shell activity, is a controller callback.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened, e.g. an IP address, a host, a process pair.

Verdicts you will have to choose between

True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The five fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by these. Learn them and the queries write themselves:

  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record. It tells you what kind of thing happened. You only need two:
    4688 = a program was started  ·  4624 = a logon succeeded  ·  4625 = a logon failed
  • process.name — the program that ran. On its own it proves nothing. cmd.exe is everywhere.
  • process.parent.name — the program that launched it. This is the field that carries the evidence.
  • process.command_line — the whole command, arguments and all. This is what tells you what the attacker was doing.
  • host.name and host.ip — which machine it happened on. source.ip is where a connection came from; destination.ip is where it went to.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

Web-server compromises always look the same: a program that should only serve web pages starts a command shell, runs a few commands to find out what the machine is, and the machine then calls an outside address. Hold that pattern in your head. By the middle of this lab you will be hunting for it.

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the file performed exactly the jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website) — and waited for each one to answer before moving on.
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “source.ip holds a network address”, that event.code is a number, that the process.* fields are exact keywords — before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded the log data — all 420 documents — and then counted them again to prove nothing was lost or doubled.
  • Created your two data views, and then read each one back to prove the index pattern really was stored. So when Kibana opens, everything is already there. You do not need to create them yourself.
  • Installed the two detection rules and waited for them to fire. The alerts you are about to read did not exist until the file did that, and it does not print ready until the alerts are really there — 3 from the first rule and 2 from the second. If a rule had matched nothing you would have been told so, instead of being handed an empty page.

Already started it twice?

Completely safe. The file notices the work is done and skips it. Your data will not load twice — which matters, because duplicate documents would double every count in the rest of this guide and ruin your findings. It also recognises its own two rules by name and will not install a second copy of either, which would double the alerts as surely as it would double the data. If it ever finds a partial pile it stops and tells you to run the file again with reset rather than making the mess worse.

What you are looking at

Do this

  1. Read Severity levels. Three critical alerts and two high ones.
  2. Find the count just above the table, next to Columns. It says 5 alerts: five separate events, not one summary.

And then scroll down to the rows themselves

The summary above is a chart. The evidence is the table underneath it, and this is where you read what actually fired.

Two different times, and the difference matters

An alert’s own timestamp is when the rule ran — a minute or two ago, because the rules are still running every minute. The log record underneath each alert happened on 22 September at 10:00, 10:02 and 10:05 UTC, and the two network records at 10:08 and 10:14 UTC. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the alerts page will keep showing them while Discover, which looks at the events themselves, shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is the next card, and it is not a fault.

Open one alert on the JSON tab and you will find two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from one alert@timestamp 2026-10-03T05:44:52.610Z the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T10:00:00.000Z the morning of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed. It is the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September.

So: an alert is a claim that something happened; the original time is the evidence for it. Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late or a rule is run against history, and if alerts were dated by the event, today’s real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones.

Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

Open the first critical alert

Click the ⇉ icon on a row whose Rule is the web-shell rule, and read what Kibana says about it.

Now look at the rules themselves

Click Rules in the left-hand menu, then the Detection rules tab. Both rules are there, and they are the last piece of context you get before you start searching.

The ruleWatchesIts own queryAlerts
IIS worker process spawning a command shellauth-* event.code: 4688 and process.parent.name: "w3wp.exe" and process.name: "cmd.exe" 3
Compromised web server calling out over HTTPSnetwork-* network.protocol: "https" and source.ip: "10.0.4.21" 2
Why the second query is worth two minutes

Because it means the alert counts and your query counts have to agree. The first rule runs the same filter as Query 3 of this guide and says 3; the second runs the same filter as Query 6 and says 2. So when those queries later return 3 and 2 you have not merely found the same answer twice — you have found the same answer the monitoring system found, by a different road. If the numbers ever disagree, one of them is wrong, and now you know which one to trust.

One thing to notice about the second rule: it is scoped to a single source address. In a real deployment you would not know that address in advance, so the rule would be a threshold query over any server talking out to somewhere unexpected. That is why the rule author’s note in rule-c2.json says so. Learn the filter, not the address.

Click the time picker at the top right, switch to the Relative tab, and set it to 1 unit Days. The five alerts come back. Some versions put a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead, which does the same job. The lab itself never changed.

What you should have now

Two rules, five alerts, risk scores 99 and 73, and one server named in the reason text. So what is wrong right now?

Pick a pile5

Choose which pile of logs to look at

which logs?2 min

First, tell Discover which pile of logs to read. You have two of your own, and only one of them is where this attack starts.

Do this

  1. Click the dropdown on the far left of the search bar — the control with the label Data view beside it. It is the one that reads auth-*.
  2. Look at the list that opens. Pick auth-*. It should already be ticked, in which case close the list again with Esc and move on.
What that dropdown actually is

A data view is a saved bookmark. It records two things: which indices to read (the pattern, e.g. auth-*) and which field holds the time (@timestamp). You have exactly two of your own, listed above.

Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile. So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of the first two, never the third.

If the dropdown is empty, or the sidebar says “no available fields” even after you pick one

Then the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run setup-lab.cmd again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it now verifies each data view by reading it back and tells you if anything is wrong instead of printing a hopeful message.

Be precise6

Read the day, and learn the one time trap

273 records3 min

You clicked Search entire time range, and the lab opened up. Before you type a single query, read this screen properly — it tells you three things you need.

What you should see now

  • The tab reads Documents (273). The number lives inside the tab name, which is where you will look for it from now on. 273 is your control total: if a later query ever returns more than 273, you have made a mistake in the query, not found a surprise.
  • The time button reads Sep 22, 2026 @ 08:00:23.191 – Sep 22, 2026 @ 17:59:00.860. That is the exact span of the day’s data — just under ten hours, ending a minute before six in the afternoon.
  • The sidebar on the left now reads 16 available fields, 1 empty field and 4 meta fields. The one empty field is process.target_name, which the index template declares but no document in this lab ever uses. An empty field is normal and does not mean anything is broken.
The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

This trips up almost everyone, so read it before you go further.

The photographs in this guide were taken with the browser set to UTC, which is how the lab stores its data — so the clock times you see in them (10:00:00.000 and so on) are the stored ones. Your own computer may be in a different timezone. If yours is 8 hours ahead of UTC, the first web-shell command that this guide calls 10:00:00.000 will appear in your table as 18:00:00.000.

So which is right? Both, and it does not matter. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs.
  • Trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount. The gaps — 2 minutes, then 3, then 3, then 6 — are identical in every timezone.
  • The counts never move at all. 273, 22, 7, 3, 14, 2 are the same in Singapore as they are in London, because the range covers all the data either way. Those are the numbers to check yourself against.
  • If you want the screen to match the pictures exactly, set your computer’s timezone to UTC before you start. Not required — but then nothing on the following cards will look out of place.

And if you ever do want a narrower window

Remember this one, and it will save you hours

An empty screen in Kibana is almost never a broken query. It is almost always the time range or the data view. Check those two first, every time.

And beware: if you ever press F5 to reload, or wander off to another page and come back, the time range can snap back to Last 15 minutes and the screen goes empty again. That is not your fault and it is not broken — just click Search entire time range again. Some analysts keep the working Discover tab open in a bookmark for exactly this reason.

Investigate7

Query 1 — every program that started

1 of 6 queries2 min

First we look at all the program starts, to see the normal shape of a normal day. Every later query narrows this one down, so this is your reference point.

Why you are running this query

You have 273 log records and no idea which ones matter. Windows records an event every time a program starts, and the number it uses for that is 4688. This query throws away the 251 logons, lockouts and logoffs and keeps only the 22 process creations.

Without a baseline you cannot spot an anomaly, because you would have nothing to say what normal looked like. And “normal” is about to become the most interesting thing on the screen.

Do this

Click inside the search bar, select whatever is there, and paste in exactly this — then press Enter:

Type this into the search bar, then press Enterevent.code: 4688
What you should see

The tab reads Documents (22), and the table fills with rows. Each row is one program that started on one of your servers that day.

What that number tells you

22 programs started across four servers that day. It sounds like a lot, but spread over ten hours and four machines it is nothing — a browser, a text editor, a task manager. This is your baseline. The attacker is somewhere inside those 22.

Before you narrow anything, take one look at the whole field list

Click the Field statistics tab — the one immediately to the right of Documents (273). It shows one row per field for everything currently in view, and it is worth five seconds now so that the next card’s version of it is not a surprise. Then click Documents (273) to come back.

The wrong turn8

Query 2 — the obvious question, and why it is a dead end

7 is not evidence3 min

The alert says the server ran command shells. So the obvious first move is to look for command shells. Do it — and then understand exactly why the answer does not help.

Why you are running this query

You want to see the cmd.exe processes the alert is talking about. If you filter on the child program’s name, you get them. This is the query a beginner writes first, every time.

It is also a dead end, and recognising that is worth more than the query.

Do this

Replace the contents of the search bar with this. Note the lower-case and and the double quotes:

Type this into the search bar, then press Enterevent.code: 4688 and process.name: "cmd.exe"
What you should see

The tab reads Documents (7). Seven command shells on your network in a working day. Now read the Summary column of the first two rows and notice something that should stop you.

Why 7 is not evidence of anything

Because a command shell is not a crime. Administrators open them, scripts open them, installers open them. Seven of them across four servers on an ordinary Tuesday is a completely normal day.

What actually matters is who started them. In these seven rows the parent is explorer.exe — a human being. The alert’s rows will have a parent that is a web server. Same event, completely different story, and the only field that tells them apart is process.parent.name.

The tool that looks like it should help, and does not

At this point most people click the Field statistics tab, because it sounds like it would summarise the parents for you. Here is what it actually does — so you recognise it:

So how do you get the split?

With the honest method that always works: ask again with one more condition and read the number off the Documents tab. That is exactly what the next card does, and it is why the two search boxes in this guide are always checked against the tab count.

One field9

Look at one field and see the whole fleet at once

search box empty2 min

Before narrowing with a query, look at the parent field on its own. This is the fastest way to understand a field, and it is worth learning because it works for every investigation you will ever do.

Do this

  1. Clear the search box completely and press Enter. You should be back to Documents (273).
  2. In the sidebar, click the words process.parent.name (not the + on the right — you will meet that button in two cards).
  3. A small panel opens under the field with its Top values. Read them.
Why this screen is the most valuable in the lab

Because it compresses 22 rows of process data into two names. Once you can see the shape of a field like that, you stop reading documents one at a time and start asking questions of the field.

It is also the honest limit of the tool, and the card before you showed you where that limit is. Use the panel to find out which values exist. Use a query to find out how many of each.

The breakthrough10

Query 3 — the parent changes everything

22 → 7 → 33 min

You have proved that 7 command shells is not an attack. Now add the one condition that turns a normal day into an incident.

Why you are running this query

You are not hunting for shells any more. You are hunting for w3wp.exe being a parent. This keeps only the program starts whose launcher was the IIS web-server worker, and throws away every other user on the network. Whatever is left is not a hunch — it is the attacker’s activity, isolated.

Do this

Type this into the search bar, then press Enterevent.code: 4688 and process.parent.name: "w3wp.exe"
What you should see

The tab reads Documents (3). The histogram above collapses to a single tall bar at 10:00 and flat everywhere else. Three program starts, all within five minutes of each other, all with the same impossible parent.

What this output actually tells you

Three separate findings, and each one matters:

  • A web server started three command shells. That combination has no innocent explanation. w3wp.exe serves HTTP requests; it does not open a cmd.exe at 10 o’clock in the morning. This is the classic web-shell fingerprint.
  • All three happened inside five minutes, and the histogram shows nothing else anywhere near. Fast, mechanical and repetitive — that is not a person, and it is not a monitoring job that went wrong.
  • You have already found the host without asking for it. Read host.name in that highlighted row: sec-win-06, at 10.0.4.21. That is the server named in the alert, and it is the only machine in the whole auth pile with only three records in it.

Compare that with the 7 shells you saw a moment ago. Same event, completely different story. That difference is the whole job.

What they ran11

Query 4 — read the commands, and add the columns

4 of 6 queries4 min

You know a web shell ran. You do not yet know what the attacker asked it to do, and that is what turns an alert into an incident report. So pin the query to the flagged server and make the command line a column of its own.

Step 1 — pin it to the server in the alert

Type this into the search bar, then press Enterevent.code: 4688 and process.parent.name: "w3wp.exe" and process.name: "cmd.exe" and host.name: "sec-win-06"

The tab should still read Documents (3). Adding the last two conditions changed nothing — which is itself a finding: every single web-shell command on the fleet ran on one host, as one account. This is the same query the companion brief instructions.md gives you in one line.

Step 2 — add the three columns you need

  1. In the sidebar, find host.name. Point at the row (hover it) and a small ⊕ button appears on the right of the row. Its real name is Add field as column. Click it.
  2. Do the same for process.command_line, then for user.name.
  3. Each one appears as a new column header, and the sidebar grows a Selected fields group at the top listing what you have added.
If the ⊕ does not appear

It only shows while your pointer is over the row. Move the mouse onto the field name and look to the far right of the row, before the edge of the sidebar. If you cannot find it after a few tries, there is a second way: the Columns button at the right-hand end of the tab bar opens a list where you tick the fields you want.

Write these five things down now

Open Notepad and record them exactly as your screen shows them. You need all five for the timeline on the Timeline card and for the report on the Write it up card.

host.name
the server — sec-win-06
host.ip
its address — 10.0.4.21 (you need the IP, not the name: the next stage searches by IP)
user.name
the account the commands ran as — IIS APPPOOL\DefaultAppPool
how many
the number in the tab — 3
the times
three timestamps, oldest first — 10:00:00.000, 10:02:00.000, 10:05:00.000 (add your own timezone offset if your screen shows one)

You still do not know whether anything came after those commands. The alert mentions outbound connections, and nothing in the auth pile can tell you about those — they are in the other pile. That is the next two cards: switch piles, then filter by the compromised address.

Go deeper12

Open one record and read every field

confirm your 5 facts3 min

The Summary column is enough to find things, but not enough to be certain. Before you write your notes, open one of the three records properly and read it field by field. This is how you avoid a report built on a half-read row.

Do this

  1. Look at the left-hand end of a row. In its own narrow column, immediately before the @timestamp column, there is a small button: two arrows pointing diagonally away from each other (⇉). Its real name is Toggle dialog with details.
  2. Click the button, not the row. Clicking anywhere else in the row does nothing at all — this is the single most common stumble in this lab.
  3. A Document panel slides in from the right. Read it.
  4. When you are finished, press Escape, or click ✕ at the top right of the panel, or Close at the bottom.
Two things in that panel that will surprise you
  • event.code is shown as 4,688 with a thousands separator, even though the field is the number 4688. You type 4688 in a query, never 4,688 — a comma will give you zero results and no error message.
  • @timestamp is shown as Sep 22, 2026 @ 10:05:00.000, not as 2026-09-22T10:05:00.000Z. Kibana reformats times for you, in your own timezone. Read it, copy it, and do not try to re-type it anywhere.

Also worth knowing: _id, _index and _score are not evidence. They are Elasticsearch’s own bookkeeping. _index will read auth-2026.09.22, which is a useful confirmation that you are in the right pile.

You have now proved the alert is not a false alarm

Every clause of the alert is in front of you, verified on screen: the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) started a command shell (cmd.exe), it ran reconnaissance commands (whoami, net user /domain, systeminfo), and it did so as the web application pool on the flagged server. The web shell exists. The only thing left is the second half of the alert: did the server call out?

The other pile13

Query 5 — all the HTTPS, and why it proves nothing

5 of 6 queries · 14 is not an answer3 min

The connections live in the other pile. Switch to it, ask the obvious question, and learn the second lesson of this lab: a destination address on its own does not identify an attacker.

Do this

  1. Click the Data view dropdown on the far left and choose network-* instead of auth-*. The sidebar changes to the network fields, and the tab now reads Documents (147).
  2. Replace the search bar contents with this, and press Enter:
Type this into the search bar, then press Enternetwork.protocol: "https"
  1. Add destination.ip as a column: hover the field in the sidebar and click its ⊕.
What you should see

The tab reads Documents (14), and the destination.ip column shows four different external addresses: 198.51.100.42, 192.0.2.10, 192.0.2.24 and 203.0.113.9. Every one of them on port 443, and every one of them from a different internal server.

Stop. This is the second dead end, and it is the more dangerous one

Your instinct is to look for “the unfamiliar external IP”. There is no such thing in this data, and here is why that matters.

198.51.100.42 receives six of the fourteen connections — more than any other address, and it is the one your eye lands on. It is not the answer: thirteen of the 147 records in this pile go to it, from four different machines, over five different protocols, at times scattered across the whole day, in the middle of ordinary work. Only two of them come from the compromised host.

That is what a known external service looks like. A controller is not identified by being the most popular destination. It is identified by being called by the machine you have already proved is compromised, and nothing else.

So always filter by the source, not just the destination. Your compromised host is 10.0.4.21. Go there.

The callback14

Query 6 — the server calls out

6 of 6 queries · controller found3 min

One condition more. Same data view, same query, plus the address of the host you have already proved is compromised.

Do this

Type this into the search bar, then press Enternetwork.protocol: "https" and source.ip: "10.0.4.21"

Add destination.port as a column too (hover it, click ⊕), so you can see the port. You should now have:

What this output actually tells you
  • The first callback is 3 minutes after the last recon command. That ordering is the evidence. The attacker ran systeminfo at 10:05, learned what the box was, and three minutes later opened a channel to fetch instructions. Cause, then effect, in that order, inside a quarter of an hour.
  • One external address, twice, and never from anywhere else in this lab. That makes 198.51.100.42 a strong IOC — something to block and to hunt for across the rest of your estate.
  • Port 443 both times, with tiny payloads (about 2 KB each). This is a beacon — a small regular call home, not data exfiltration. Worth saying in the report: the attacker had not started stealing anything yet.

Add these to your notes: the controller IP 198.51.100.42, the port 443, the count 2, and the two timestamps.

That is the whole chain. Now put it in order.

Six queries, and every clause of the incident is on the record. The next card turns them into a timeline, which is the part of a report that nobody can argue with.

Put it together15

Build the timeline

most important 5 min

This is the most important 5 minutes in the lab. Investigators do not just collect facts — they arrange them so the facts argue the conclusion for them.

Do this

Open a text file (Notepad is fine) and write five lines, oldest first, copying the times off your own screen. The yellow blank on the first line is your work: type in the clock time your table shows, and check it against the row you clicked. Everything after it is pre-filled — the commands, the hosts and the gaps — because the gaps are the same in every timezone and they are the actual evidence.

  1. your screen  →  type the first timestamp here  ·  first command
    w3wp.exe started cmd.exe running cmd.exe /c whoami on sec-win-06 as IIS APPPOOL\DefaultAppPool. — who am I? This is the first event of the whole incident, and it is the same moment the first alert points at through kibana.alert.original_time.
  2. +2 min
    Second cmd.exe, same parent, same host, running cmd.exe /c net user /domain. — who else is in this domain?
  3. +3 min
    Third cmd.exe, running cmd.exe /c systeminfo. — what is this machine? The attacker now knows the host, the domain and the machine.
  4. +3 min
    Outbound HTTPS to 198.51.100.42:443 from 10.0.4.21. — the server calling its controller, three minutes after the last command. This is the alert that carries risk score 73.
  5. +6 min
    Second outbound HTTPS to the same address, 198.51.100.42:443, about 2 KB each time. — the beacon repeating.

The gaps are pre-filled as +2, +3, +3, +6 minutes and the whole sequence is 14 minutes long. If your screen shows a different offset from this guide, write down your clock times instead — what matters is that the five lines stay in this order and keep these gaps, because a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount and moves none of the gaps.

The same five lines as a table

So you can see the shape of the answer in one glance, and copy it straight into the Timeline section of your report. These are the stored times, in UTC:

Time (UTC)GapSourceWhat happenedWhich alert
10:00:00.000—auth-* w3wp.exe → cmd.exe /c whoami on sec-win-06 critical, risk 99
10:02:00.000+2 minauth-* w3wp.exe → cmd.exe /c net user /domain critical, risk 99
10:05:00.000+3 minauth-* w3wp.exe → cmd.exe /c systeminfo critical, risk 99
10:08:00.000+3 minnetwork-* HTTPS callback 10.0.4.21 → 198.51.100.42:443 high, risk 73
10:14:00.000+6 minnetwork-* second HTTPS callback to the same address high, risk 73
The shape of the answer

All five events fall inside a 14-minute window on a single day, at the tail of the working day. Nothing is hours apart, nothing is days apart, and nothing else in either pile happens anywhere near those three commands. That tightness is itself evidence — it rules out coincidence, a monitoring job, and routine administration.

And the order is the argument: shell, then reconnaissance, then a call home. A monitoring script does not do that. An administrator does not do that as the web application pool on a public web server.

Then ask the five questions that turn facts into a verdict

QuestionYour answer, and the query that proved it
How did they get in?parent = w3wp.exe on a web server — they uploaded a web shell. Query 3.
Where did it land?sec-win-06 (10.0.4.21) — the IIS server named in the alert. Query 3 and Query 4.
What did they do?3 commands: whoami, net user /domain, systeminfo. Query 4.
Where did they go next?2 HTTPS callbacks to 198.51.100.42:443. Query 6.
How much damage?None shown. No file writes, no privilege change, no lateral movement — the callbacks are about 2 KB each.
The one-sentence verdict

Between 10:00 and 10:14 on 22 September 2026, an attacker who had uploaded a web shell to the IIS server sec-win-06 (10.0.4.21) ran three reconnaissance commands through the web server’s own application-pool identity, then made two outbound HTTPS connections to a single external address, 198.51.100.42, on port 443.

That is a true positive. Every clause of that sentence is traceable to one of the six queries you just ran, to one of the two rules that fired, and every number in it is a number you read off your own screen.

25 mindo not skip

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in this guide you type. Do this yourself, and do it now

Your verdict in one line

Two things worth double-checking in your own report

These are the two that catch people out, so read yours back now:

  1. Did you narrow to the parent process? A report that stops at “event.code: 4688 returned 22 rows, and program starts look normal” is incomplete. You had to add process.parent.name: "w3wp.exe" before the picture appeared, and the event code on its own is not a finding.
  2. Did you filter the network side by source? If you stopped at “198.51.100.42 is the strangest destination”, you have proved nothing: other machines in this lab talk to that address too, on five different protocols, all day. The controller is only identified because the compromised host called it and nothing else did.

And one bonus: if you noticed that the two alerts carry different risk scores (99 for the web shell, 73 for the callback), say so in your report and explain why you agree or disagree with the ordering. It is not required, and nothing checks it automatically, but it is the sentence that turns a list of counts into a judgement.

Anything you left blank is written in as [not answered] rather than quietly dropped, so a hole cannot turn into a tidy-looking submission. The PDF lands in your Downloads folder; nothing is uploaded and no internet connection is needed.

Finish17

Tear the lab down

one file1 min

One file removes everything the lab created, and nothing else. This matters: the lab stores its data in a Docker volume, and volumes are not removed when you close a window or shut down your computer. Left behind, it silently occupies disk space until someone deletes it by hand.

Do this

  1. Make sure you have exported your submission from the previous card. The teardown deletes the data, and the data cannot be re-created without running setup again.
  2. Close your browser and every Kibana tab.
  3. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  4. It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  5. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what was kept.

What it deletes — and what it does not

ObjectNameWhy
Containerwebshell-iis-001-elasticsearchThe database process
Containerwebshell-iis-001-kibanaThe website process
Networkwebshell-iis-001_labThe private network they shared
Volumewebshell-iis-001_esdataAll 420 log documents, both detection rules and all five alerts — the disk space
Filedocker-compose.ymlThe generated compose file. The setup file rewrites it.
Folderelklab-webshell-iis-001Temporary files the setup made

On Windows the scratch folder sits in %TEMP%; on macOS and Linux it is in your temp directory. The names are the same everywhere, and only the names are ever deleted.

What it deliberately keeps
  • The Elasticsearch and Kibana images. These are the big downloads — about a gigabyte. Keeping them means the next time you run this lab, the setup file starts in seconds instead of twenty minutes.
  • Everything else on your computer. Other Docker projects, other labs, your images, your other volumes — all untouched.
  • Your files. The log data, the templates, rule.json and rule-c2.json are all still in the folder afterwards.

Every object name above begins with this lab’s own folder name (webshell-iis-001). That is not a coincidence — it is how the file guarantees it can only ever delete its own lab. It never runs docker system prune and it never deletes an image.

What you should see

The last thing the teardown file prints Verifying... gone container webshell-iis-001-elasticsearch gone container webshell-iis-001-kibana gone volume webshell-iis-001_esdata gone file .../webshell-iis-001-/docker-compose.yml gone folder .../elklab-webshell-iis-001 ============================================================== The "webshell-iis-001" lab has been removed. Kept on purpose: every Docker image, and every other container and volume on this machine.

Yours will show a different path — a Windows path on Windows, a /var/folders/... or /tmp/ one on a Mac. If anything is still listed, the file prints a WARNING line naming it and the exact command that removes it, rather than pretending it succeeded.

If you would rather just stop it and keep the data

Sometimes you want the lab back tomorrow without waiting for it to reload. Stop the containers but keep everything, and start them again later with one command:

Run this in a terminal, in the lab folderdocker compose -f docker-compose.yml down

Your data lives in the Docker volume, so it survives — and so do the alerts. Bring it all back with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d, or simply run the setup file again — it is safe to run twice and will not re-import anything, install a second copy of either rule, or raise a second set of alerts.

Running teardown twice is harmless

It checks what is actually there first, tells you there is nothing to do, and exits. It will not complain and it will not go looking for something else to delete. That matters, because people run it twice to be sure.

Reference18

If something goes wrong

not a steplook me up

Six things account for almost every problem in this lab. Work down the list rather than guessing, and do them in order — the first one explains most cases.

1. The Alerts page is empty

Symptom: Security → Alerts opens, and there is nothing in the table even though the rules exist under Rules.

Cause: the time picker. An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, which is today, so a range that has been narrowed to yesterday loses it. Set the page’s time picker to Relative, 1 day (or Last 24 hours).

Also possible: the rule fired before the data was imported and will not fire again for the same records, because a rule only looks at new data. Run the setup file again — it verifies the alert counts and tells you if the page really is short.

2. The screen is empty and no Documents (n) tab appears

Symptom: “No results match your search criteria”, and Search entire time range on the screen.

Cause: the time range. Discover opens on Last 15 minutes and your data is from 22 September 2026.

Fix: click Search entire time range. You should immediately see Documents (273). If you instead pressed F5 or navigated back to this page, do this again — the range resets on reload.

3. A query returns 0, but the same query worked a moment ago

Symptom: you changed the search bar and now nothing comes back.

Cause, in order of likelihood:

  • The data view changed. A network query run against auth-* will always return 0, and vice versa. Check the dropdown on the far left.
  • The time range changed. Check the time button.
  • A comma crept into a number. The screen shows 4,688 but you must type 4688. A comma returns 0 with no error message.
  • AND was typed in capitals, or and in a field name. KQL wants lower-case and, or, not.
  • A missing double quote around w3wp.exe, cmd.exe, https or an IP address.

Fix: select all of the search bar, delete it, and paste the query again from this page using the COPY button. That rules out every typing mistake at once.

4. The counts are doubled

Symptom: you see 546 instead of 273, 294 instead of 147, or 10 alerts instead of 5.

Cause: something was imported or installed twice — usually the old curl import from an earlier version of this lab run by hand after the setup file had already done it.

Fix: run the setup file with reset (Windows: setup-lab.cmd reset; macOS and Linux: ./setup-lab.sh reset). It removes the containers, the volume and everything in them, then rebuilds from scratch. It will not import on top of a half-full index, and it recognises its own two rules by name, so it will not install a second copy of either.

5. The sidebar says “No available fields containing data”, or the Data view list is empty

Cause: the data views were not created, or were created with an empty index pattern. A data view with an empty pattern matches no index at all, so Discover shows zero fields and no results — with no visible reason, which is why it confuses people.

Fix: run the setup file again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it now reads each data view back and resolves it against the index, failing with a plain-English message if the stored pattern is wrong instead of printing a hopeful line and leaving you stuck.

6. The setup file refuses to start
What the setup file saysWhat to do
docker was not foundDocker is not installed. Ask your instructor.
Docker is installed but the engine is not respondingOpen Docker Desktop and wait until it says it is running, then run the file again.
something else is already using port 9200Another lab is running. The script refuses to touch it, correctly. Stop the other one, or run the teardown file from the folder that owns it.
a container called webshell-iis-001-elasticsearch already existsThe folder was copied. The script will not destroy the other copy; it prints the exact commands to remove it by hand.
Elasticsearch did not become ready in timeIt prints the last 40 lines of the container log. Usually not enough memory for Docker; close other applications, or give Docker Desktop more memory in its settings.
the auth index holds N documents but this lab ships 273A partial load. The script refuses to import on top of it, because that would create duplicates. Run it again with reset.
the rules are installed but the Alerts page does not hold 5 alertsThe rules exist but have not fired yet, or cannot see the data. Check docker logs webshell-iis-001-kibana for the rule’s execution status, and remember both rules only look back 365 days.
Two more things that look like errors but are not
  • “1 empty field” in the sidebar. That is process.target_name: declared in the index template, used by no document in this lab. Perfectly normal.
  • The alert timestamps are today, and the log timestamps are from 22 September 2026. Not a bug and not a mismatch: an alert is dated when the rule ran, and a log record is dated when the thing happened. Use the record’s time in your report. Times are also printed in your computer’s timezone, so the counts and the gaps are unaffected.

And if you are completely stuck, the setup file is idempotent: you cannot make it worse by running it again.

The 30-second checklist

Data view right? → Time range says a date, not “Last 15 minutes”? → Query text in the bar? → Number in the Documents tab matches the number this guide quotes? If all four are true and something still looks wrong, press F5 and re-click Search entire time range, then re-run the queries from the top. If Query 1 does not return 22 documents, your time range is still wrong; if it does, the problem is in the query text rather than in the dates.

Yellow, dashed is the opposite: a value that is deliberately not printed here, because finding it is your job. Type it into the box on the timeline card.

Stuck on a step?

Almost every problem in this lab has one of six causes, and all six are covered on the If something goes wrong card near the end: an empty Alerts page, the time range, the data view, a typing mistake in the query, doubled data, or a setup that would not start. Go there rather than guessing.
